paper_title: PixelDense: Dense Prediction as Representation Alignment for Pixel Diffusion

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Representation alignment (REPA) accelerates diffusion transformer training, but its alignment targets are almost exclusively semantic encoders such as DINOv2 and CLIP. Recent analysis points to spatial structure, not global semantics, as the carrier of the alignment effect, yet dense-prediction foundation models trained to predict that structure remain overlooked as REPA targets. In pixel-space diffusion, SAM2, Depth Anything v2, and Metric3D v2 each outperform the DINOv2-only GenEval baseline, with the two geometric teachers leading the segmentation teacher. A flat sum of all four teachers, however, lands below the best single geometric teacher, as semantic and geometric gradients compete for one denoiser projection. We introduce PixelDense, which routes DINOv2 and SAM2 through a semantic projection stream, routes Depth Anything v2 and Metric3D v2 through a geometric projection stream, and adds a weight-space orthogonality penalty that keeps the two streams in disjoint subspaces. All four teachers are frozen during training and dropped at inference. Applied to PixelGen and DeCo with a single recipe, PixelDense improves GenEval, DPG-Bench, and HPS v2.1, raises PixelGen-XXL's GenEval Overall from 0.7927 to 0.8093, and beats every single-teacher and unfactored multi-teacher variant. In partial-noise reconstruction, independent panoptic, depth, and surface-normal probes show up to 53.1% PQ gain and 36.0% depth AbsRel reduction at $τ=0.5$ across COCO and Flickr30K. From random initialization, PixelDense also reaches the baseline's peak GenEval 1.23x faster. In SDEdit editing on PIE-Bench, PixelDense keeps more of the source background and layout at every edit strength, raising background PSNR by up to 2.2 dB.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Dense-prediction foundation models can now extract increasingly rich spatial structure from single RGB image: object-level semantic features from DINOv2 [37], instance and region boundaries from SAM2 [22, 43], monocular depth from Depth Anything v2 [59, 60], and metric surface normals from Metric3D v2 [16]. Together, they capture object semantics, boundaries, depth, and surface orientation, jointly providing semantic and geometric constraints on what realistic image should look like. We therefore ask whether such semantic and geometric knowledge can directly supervise image generation during training, without requiring dense-prediction outputs at inference. The recent REPresentation Alignment (REPA) [61] provides direct way to use frozen encoder to supervise diffusion training. By matching intermediate denoiser features to frozen encoder features, REPA accelerates DiT training by an order of magnitude without changing inference. However, REPA-style alignment has primarily relied on semantic encoders such as DINOv2 and CLIP [42]. iREPA [46] shows that REPA-style alignment benefits primarily from the spatial structure rather than the global semantics of the teacher encoder. This suggests that dense-prediction foundation models may provide stronger structural guidance for diffusion models, as they are explicitly trained to capture spatial structures. Although video diffusion has explored geometric [53] and multi-encoder [23] alignment for temporal consistency, it remains unclear how to use semantic and geometric encoders as structural constraints for realistic image synthesis. We instantiate this idea in the setting of pixel-space diffusion, where the denoiser tokens lie on the RGB patch grid that dense teachers consume, so each token aligns directly with the teacher feature. On PixelGen [35] text-to-image backbone fine-tuned at 512512, we show that each of SAM2, Depth Anything v2, and Metric3D v2 improves GenEval Overall over the DINOv2-only baseline when used as the added alignment target, and the two geometric teachers outperform the segmentation teacher. This matches iREPAs finding that spatial structure carries the alignment signal. However, dense teachers do not compose under flat sum. four-way summed REPA loss across DINOv2, SAM2, Depth Anything v2, and Metric3D v2 through single denoiser projection lands below the best single geometric teacher, diluting the fine-grained structure that motivated adding more teachers in the first place. The cause is that semantic and geometric teachers reward incompatible invariances. Semantic encoders push toward viewpoint invariance and instance identity, while geometric encoders push toward metric layout and surface orientation. When both groups of gradients share single feature basis, the denoiser cannot allocate distinct subspaces to distinct kinds of structure, and the teachers compete instead of compose. The core challenge is therefore representation routing. Semantic and geometric teachers must supervise the same denoiser through separate subspaces while the RGB sampler stays unchanged. Dense perception offers richer alignment supervision than semantic encoders alone, but only if the alignment objective respects the semantic and geometric structure of the teacher bank. We propose PixelDense, factored dense-alignment framework that provides this structure. It decomposes the multi-teacher objective into two disjoint streams: semantic stream that carries DINOv2 and SAM2 through shared semantic projection bottleneck, and geometric stream that carries Depth Anything v2 and Metric3D through separate geometric projection bottleneck. weight-space orthogonality regularizer on the two bottlenecks input projections keeps the denoiser from collapsing them into common subspace, so the two streams specialize rather than average. The teachers remain frozen and are dropped at inference, so PixelDense adds no cost to sampling. PixelDense is not tied to particular pixel-space backbone. We instantiate it on PixelGen and on DeCo [34], two pixel diffusion transformers with different loss recipes, and the same alignment recipe transfers without modification. On PixelGen at 512512, full PixelDense raises GenEval Overall over the DINOv2-only baseline from 0.7927 to 0.8093, 2.09% relative gain, and beats every single-teacher and unfactored multi-teacher variant we compare against. It also preserves sourceimage structure more faithfully than PixelGen in partial-noise reconstruction. Under standalone segmentation, depth, and surface-normal probes, PixelDense has better scores in every COCO and Flickr30K setting in Table 2. At τ = 0.5, panoptic PQ rises by 35.3% against COCO panoptic annotations and by 53.1% against Flickr30K pseudo labels. Depth AbsRel falls by up to 36.0%. On DeCo, PixelDense also improves over the baseline. The same structure preservation carries over to image editing: with SDEdit on PIE-Bench, PixelDense keeps more of the source background and layout at every edit strength. 2 The main contributions of this work are summarized as follows: We introduce PixelDense, dense-perception representation-alignment framework for pixelspace diffusion. PixelDense uses semantic, segmentation, depth, and surface-normal models as training-time teachers while retaining the original RGB generator for inference. We propose semanticgeometric factorization for dense teacher banks. PixelDense routes DINOv2 and SAM2 through semantic projection stream, routes Depth Anything v2 and Metric3D v2 through geometric projection stream, and uses weight space orthogonality to keep the two forms of supervision from collapsing into the same denoiser subspace. We identify negative-transfer effect in dense multi-teacher alignment. Although each dense teacher improves over the DINOv2-only baseline, simply summing semantic and geometric REPA losses forces incompatible invariances through shared projection and degrades the combined signal. This reframes teacher composition as representation-routing problem. Extensive experiments demonstrate the effectiveness and transferability of PixelDense. On PixelGen and DeCo, PixelDense improves compositional generation over matched fine-tunes, single-teacher alignment, and unfactored multi-teacher baselines. In partialnoise reconstruction, standalone segmentation, depth, and surface-normal estimators show stronger structure preservation on COCO and Flickr30K, and this carries over to SDEdit image editing on PIE-Bench.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Diffusion models for image generation. Diffusion models [14, 47] and flow matching [29, 31] now form common image synthesis framework, and classifier-free guidance [13] has become standard conditioning tool. Latent diffusion [44] made compressed VAE space the default for efficient generation, while transformer denoisers including DiT [38], U-ViT [2], SiT [33], MDT [8], and DDT [50] improved the backbone. Pixel-space methods remove the VAE bottleneck and its reconstruction artifacts. Simple Diffusion [15], PixelFlow [5], and self-supervised pretraining [24] show that direct raw-pixel training is viable, and JiT [26], DeCo [34], PixelDiT [62], PixelGen [35], and Latent Forcing [1] further improve prediction targets, frequency treatment, architectures, perceptual losses, or trajectory design. These methods strengthen the denoisers, but their supervision remains an RGB reconstruction target, which leaves the semantic and geometric structure of the image implicit. We build on this pixel-space line and ask what additional training signal can supervise the denoiser. Representation alignment for diffusion models. REPA [61] answers this question by matching intermediate denoiser features to frozen encoder such as DINOv2 [37], accelerating DiT training with no inference cost. iREPA [46] further identified spatial structure as the active ingredient of the alignment signal, which reframes alignment as question about which encoder exposes that structure most directly. Follow-up work extends the recipe through VAE tuning (REPA-E [25]), hierarchical alignment (SARA [3]), time-limited objectives (HASTE [51], ERW [30], curriculum decay [49]), and entanglement or self-alignment variants (REG [52], LayerSync [10]), while PixelREPA [45] and V-Co [27] study pixel-space collapse and co-denoising. Closer to us, Align4Gen [23] and Geometry Forcing [53] bring multi-encoder geometry-aware alignment to video diffusion, but they target temporal consistency and sum teacher signals without addressing the conflict between semantic and geometric supervision. Image-generation alignment still defaults to single semantic teachers such as DINOv2, CLIP [42], and SigLIP [63], leaving open which encoders actually carry the spatial structure iREPA points to. Dense prediction meets generation. Dense prediction foundation models, including SAM [22] and SAM2 [43] for segmentation, Depth Anything [59] and Depth Anything V2 [60] for depth, and Metric3D v2 [16] for depth and surface normals, are trained explicitly to expose this spatial structure from single RGB image. Most prior work explores the reverse direction. Marigold [20], GeoWizard [7], Lotus [12], GenPercept [55], VPD [64], and ODISE [56] repurpose diffusion features for dense perception, while UniGS [41], SemFlow [48], UDPDiff [58], and Diff-2-in-1 [65] couple image and dense outputs in unified generators. These models still emit dense predictions or target perception gains. We take the opposite direction and use these frozen discriminative encoders as alignment teachers for pixel-space generator, routing semantic and geometric supervision through separate streams so the two forms of structure specialize rather than average, and the dense teachers are dropped at inference. 3 Figure 2: PixelDense factors dense-prediction supervision into semantic stream and geometric stream. The pixel diffusion denoiser fθ takes the noisy image xt and Qwen3 text embedding y, and reads its block-8 token state into two parallel projections, Ds = 768 semantic projection Wsem aligned to frozen DINOv2 and SAM2 features, and Dg = 1024 geometric projection Wgeo aligned to frozen Depth Anything v2 and Metric3D v2 features. weight-space orthogonality penalty Lorth on the rows of Wsem and Wgeo keeps the two streams from collapsing into shared subspace of the denoiser feature. Only the denoiser, the projections, and the per-teacher heads receive gradients. The four dense teachers are frozen during training and dropped at inference, so the deployed model is the original three-channel RGB generator with its original sampler.

sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: We first introduce the experimental setting: pixel-space backbones, dense teachers, fine-tuning recipe, datasets, metrics, and baselines. We then evaluate PixelDense on PixelGen-XXL [35] and test whether partial-noise reconstructions preserve scene geometry under independent panoptic, depth, and surface-normal predictors. Next, we analyze how each dense teacher contributes to generation quality, study multi-teacher composition, and ablate the semanticgeometric factorization, projection width, alignment block, alignment-loss weights, and orthogonality regularizer. Finally, we examine training from scratch, transfer the same recipe to DeCo [34] without retuning, test the trained model on image editing, and provide qualitative visualization under matched prompts and samplers. 4.1 Setup Our main backbone is the 1.1B PixelGen-XXL [35]. We also finetune DeCo [34] for testing the generality. Both models are pretrained with DINOv2 REPA [61]. During fine-tuning, this DINOv2 signal remains active. Because both backbones already retain the original DINOv2 REPA signal during fine-tuning, our primary comparison baseline is therefore single teacher DINOv2 baseline. We conduct all experiments on 2 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. Each GPU uses batch size of 16 with gradient accumulation of 8, giving an effective total batch size of 256. We train for 10,000 optimizer steps with AdamW and learning rate of 1e-5. At inference, we use classifier-free guidance of 4.0. We use four frozen dense prediction perception models as alignment targets. DINOv2-B/14 [37] provides object-level semantic features. SAM2 Hiera-L [43] provides segmentation aware boundary features from the last image-encoder layer. Depth Anything v2 ViT-L [60] provides monocular depth features from layer 17. Metric3D v2 ViT-L [16] provides surface normal features from layer 17. We align all teacher signals at block 8 of the diffusion denoiser. All four teachers remain frozen during training and are dropped at inference. The finetuning dataset follows the third stage of PixelGen training and uses BLIP3-o-60K [4]. We report results on GenEval [9], DPG-Bench [17], and HPS v2.1 [54]. We compare with pixel-space methods, including PixelDiT [62], PixelFlow [5], PixelGen [35], and DeCo [34]. We also include latent-space reference methods, SDXL [40] and SD3 [6]. 4.2 Results As shown in Table 1, PixelDense improves over the matched finetune of PixelGen across GenEval Overall, DPG-Bench, and HPS v2.1. It raises GenEval Overall from 0.7927 to 0.8093, 2.09% relative gain over the baseline. The gains land on the compositional axes that touch object boundaries, depth layout, and surface geometry, which are the axes that dense-prediction supervision is designed to lift. Compared to the listed pixel-space backbones at this scale, PixelDense reaches the strongest GenEval Overall. The dense teachers are removed at test time, so inference speed is not changed. This agrees with iREPAs finding that spatial structure carries the alignment signal [46]. The naive four-teacher REPA sum performs worse than the best single dense REPA teacher. Shrinking both streams to smaller shared width removes capacity needed by the geometric teachers, while equalizing them at the larger width wastes semantic-stream parameters. Both variants underperform the default PixelDense configuration. Alignment Block. The mid-network tap is strongest, consistent with REPA [61]. sections.title: 5 Limitation and Conclusion
sections.content: This paper introduces PixelDense, dense-perception representation-alignment framework for pixelspace diffusion. Our approach routes semantic and geometric teachers through separate streams, using weight-space orthogonality to prevent collapse into single denoiser subspace. Experiments on PixelGen and DeCo show improved compositional alignment at no inference-time cost, while reconstruction probes show stronger preservation of segmentation, depth, and surface-normal structure. Image editing typically requires modifying content while maintaining source image identity, layout, and 3D structure. With SDEdit on PIE-Bench, PixelDense keeps more of the source background and layout at every edit strength, so it is promising approach for scenarios that demand strict structure preservation. Our editing tests cover only SDEdit, and other editing methods, such as inversion-based and instruction-based editing, are left to future work. We hope PixelDense encourages using dense perception models as practical training-time supervision for image generators.

sections.title: A Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1 Pixel-Space Backbones The primary backbone is PixelGen-XXL [35], 1.1B-parameter pixel-space diffusion transformer with 16 visual blocks. Inputs are 512 512 RGB images split into 32 32 patches, giving = 256 visual tokens of hidden width dh = 1536. The text branch uses frozen Qwen3 text encoder [57] with cross-attention into the visual stream. The transfer backbone is DeCo-T2I [34], 1.1B pixel diffusion transformer with the same patch grid. Both backbones are pretrained with single-teacher DINOv2 [37] REPA [61] and continue to receive that signal during PixelDense fine-tuning. The deployed sampler reads only the three RGB channels, so PixelDense adds no parameters at inference. A.2 Frozen Dense Teachers The four teachers and the block used for alignment are summarized in Table 7. Each teacher consumes the clean image scaled to [0, 1] at 512 512, and emits token grid that is bilinearly resampled to the denoisers 16 16 patch lattice and channel-wise L2 normalized before the cosine alignment of Equations (1) and (5). Teacher weights remain frozen, no augmentation is applied at the teacher input, and gradients flow only through the denoiser, the projection streams, and the per-teacher heads. Feature dimension is the per-token width before normalization. Group is the semantic-versus-geometric assignment used by Section 3.3. Teacher Feature dim. Each stream is two-layer MLP of the form (2)σ(LN(W hℓ,n)), with SiLU nonlinearity σ and channel-wise LayerNorm. The semantic stream uses Wsem R768dh followed by (2) geo R10241024. The four teacher heads gDINO, gSAM, gDA2, gM3D are single linear maps from the corresponding stream width to the teacher feature dimension in Table 7. The optimizer is AdamW with β1 = 0.9, β2 = 0.999, weight decay 0.01, learning rate 1e-5, and constant schedule after 200-step linear warmup. Each fine-tune runs for 10,000 optimizer steps, which is the budget reported in Tables 1 and 3 to 5. The full objective of Equation (7) combines the flow-matching loss LFM, the four cosine alignment losses with the weights in Equation (6), the orthogonality penalty with λorth = 0.01, and the auxiliary LPIPS and Perceptual-DINO losses inherited from PixelGen. We use bf16 mixed precision, gradient norm clipping at 1.0, and exponential moving average over denoiser parameters with decay 0.9999. The same recipe transfers to DeCo without retuning. The from-scratch run of Figure 4 trains pixel diffusion model from random initialization at 128 128 on BLIP3-o-60K [4] with the same effective batch size and optimizer, for 100,000 steps with and without PixelDense. 15 A.5 Sampling At inference, the dense teachers and the alignment-side parameters Φ are dropped. We use the Adam LM solver with 25 steps and classifier-free guidance scale 4.0. Generation resolution is 512 512 for PixelGen-XXL and DeCo, and 128 128 for the from-scratch run. Reported numbers are seed-matched per evaluation, so PixelGen, the matched fine-tune, and PixelDense receive the same prompts and sampler. A.6 Datasets Fine-tuning uses BLIP3-o-60K [4], the third-stage dataset of PixelGen training, with no extra filtering. The from-scratch run uses the same dataset at 128 128. Evaluation uses GenEval [9], DPGBench [17], and HPS v2.1 [54] for text-to-image quality, COCO 2017 [28] val and Flickr30K [39] test for partial-noise reconstruction. All evaluation images are pre-resized with bilinear interpolation to 512 512 followed by center crop, and GT panoptic masks are nearest resampled with the same crop so that pixel indices align across reconstruction, prediction, and reference. We did not retrain or fine-tune any teacher, probe, or evaluation model.

sections.title: B Evaluation Protocols
sections.content: B.1 Text-to-Image Benchmarks GenEval [9] is run with the released 553 prompt set across the six standard categories of single-object, two-object, counting, colors, attribute binding, and position. Score with the official GenEval scorer, and report Overall together with the six per-category scores. DPG-Bench [17] is run with its official prompt set, four images per prompt, and the released grader. HPS v2.1 [54] is run on the four 800-prompt style splits of Anime, Concept-art, Paintings, and Photo, with one image per prompt. The per-style breakdown for our PixelGen-XXL fine-tunes is given in Table 15. B.2 Partial-Noise Reconstruction Probes The probe of Table 2 corrupts an input image x0 by xt = (1 τ )x0 + τ ε with ε (0, I), feeds xt together with caption to the model, and reads the predicted clean image ˆx0. Captions are the original COCO caption with the lowest sentence index for COCO, and the first non-empty Flickr30K caption otherwise. For each τ {0.5, 0.7, 0.9} we use single fixed Gaussian sample ε shared across PixelGen and PixelDense, so the two models reconstruct from identical noisy inputs. Panoptic probes. The same OneFormer [18] model with two backbones, Swin-L [32] and DiNATL [11] pretrained on COCO panoptic for 100 epochs, is applied to the reconstruction ˆx0 and the reference, both at 512 512. Real-COCO references are the public panoptic GT after nearest resize and the same center crop. Pseudo references are the OneFormer prediction on the resize-cropped original. We score with PQ [21] and mIoU under the COCO panoptic vocabulary, and average across Swin-L and DiNAT-L for the cells of Table 2. Per-backbone numbers and PQth/PQst breakdowns are in Tables 11 and 12. Depth probe. We run Marigold v1.1 depth [20] on the reconstruction ˆx0 and on the resize-cropped original. The original prediction is treated as pseudo-reference because COCO and Flickr30K do not ship dense metric depth. sections.content: C.1 Semantic versus Geometric Teacher Features Figure 6 visualizes the per-patch responses of the four dense teachers on the same image. Semantic teachers fire on object regions and instance boundaries, while geometric teachers trace depth-ordered silhouettes and surface-normal layout. The split motivates the semantic-versus-geometric factorization of Section 3.3. Figure 6: Semantic and geometric teachers light up complementary spatial structure on the same image. The leftmost column shows the RGB input, and the next four columns show the per-patch RMS magnitude of spatially normalized features from DINOv2, SAM2, Depth Anything v2, and Metric3D v2, with yellow marking high response. DINOv2 fires on object regions and SAM2 fires on instance boundaries, while Depth Anything v2 traces depth-ordered silhouettes and Metric3D v2 traces surface-normal layout. C.2 Training-Dynamics Diagnostic for Unfactored versus Factored Alignment This subsection looks at the training trajectories. We log the four per-teacher cosine alignment losses every 50 optimizer steps and read the four curves jointly across runs from Table 3, the naive equal-weight sum and our default PixelDense configuration. The diagnostic examines three properties simultaneously, namely whether the four teachers co-improve over the full training, whether they move in lockstep at the optimizer-step scale, and whether each teachers signal is being absorbed at similar rate. Setup. Both runs share the recipe of Section 4.1. We log every 50 optimizer steps from step 49 to step 9,999, giving 200 points per run for each of LDINO, LSAM, LDA2, and LM3D. We compute three diagnostics on this 200 4 matrix per run. Pearson correlation on the centered curves measures whether the four losses co-improve over the full schedule. Cosine similarity of step-to-step loss deltas measures whether the four losses move together or apart at the optimizer-step scale. Per-teacher relative loss reduction, taken between the first ten and last ten logged points, measures how much of each teachers signal the denoiser has absorbed. Under PixelDense the DINOv2 reduction settles at 78.49%, the Depth Anything v2 reduction rises from 72.81% to 77.49%, and the Metric3D normal reduction rises from 64.26% to 69.37%. Each loss is being absorbed at rate more uniform across the bank, with no teacher under-served, and the higher mean reduction is achieved without requiring more than 4.6-point relative drop on the dominant DINOv2 term. What the diagnostic says about knowledge transmission. The diagnostic is consistent with the structural argument of Section 3.3. An unfactored objective sums four teacher cosine gradients on the same denoiser hidden state without reserving semantic and geometric subspaces. This can align per-step loss deltas across the bank and leave slower teachers behind on the longer horizon, which is why the naive run shows both higher cross-teacher step-delta cosine and larger semantic-versusgeometric reduction gap. Factoring the objective across the semantic-versus-geometric supervision split lets the per-step gradient match the active teacher group with less drag from the other group, which is what the lower cross-stream step-delta cosine measures. The separated update shows up as larger and more uniform per-teacher loss reductions over 10,000 steps, which we read as more even knowledge transmission from the four frozen teachers into the denoiser. The training-time advantage in Tables 8 and 10 is the mechanism behind the GenEval gap reported in Table 3. sections.title: E Broader Impact and Limitations
sections.content: PixelDense improves the training-time supervision of pixel-space text-to-image diffusion models without changing the deployed sampler. Like other text-to-image generators, the resulting models can support creative tools and accessible visual prototyping, and can also be misused for fabricated imagery, identity-targeted content, or copyright-sensitive style mimicry. The teachers we add are perception models trained on natural images, so PixelDense inherits whatever biases are present in those teachers training distributions on top of the biases of the pixel backbone.
